title: Malthusianism

definition.text: The theory that population can grow exponentially while food and other resources grow only steadily, so living standards eventually fall until population declines.

facts.text: It stems from Thomas Robert Malthus's 1798 An Essay on the Principle of Population.
Malthus argued that technology could raise resources and living standards, but the extra abundance would fuel population growth until resources per person fell back to their old level.
A Malthusian catastrophe, or Malthusian trap, is predicted if population outpaces farm output, causing famine or war.

Evidence fits the pre-industrial era: from 1 to 1500 AD better technology raised population density but not living standards, and a labourer's daily wage bought about 15 pounds of wheat in ancient Babylonia and 13 in England in 1800.
After World War II, mechanised farming and the Green Revolution greatly raised crop yields, and most developed countries' populations grew slower than productivity.
Many models of resource depletion are Malthusian in character, predicting that consumption will outstrip new supply and cause a crisis.
Critics such as William Hazlitt argued Malthus confused natural limits on output with the artificial way society distributes it.

contested_note: Critics from Ricardo onward have disputed Malthus's theory, and 20th-century growth did not produce the predicted catastrophe.

definition.text: Malthus's two kinds of brake on population: preventive checks that lower birth rates and positive checks that shorten lives.

facts.text: Preventive checks include celibacy and chastity; positive checks are chiefly war, plague and famine, but also poor health and economic conditions.
When positive checks cause high rates of premature death, the result is called a Malthusian catastrophe.

definition.text: The concern that overpopulation and overconsumption will deplete resources and degrade the environment until ecosystems collapse.

facts.text: Post-war crop gains were followed by rapid population growth, prompting Paul R. Ehrlich and others to predict an imminent Malthusian catastrophe.
A 2004 study including Kenneth Arrow and Paul Ehrlich found that sustainability concerns had shifted from population growth to the balance between consumption and saving.
Herman Daly and Jeremy Rifkin raised neo-Malthusian concerns about modern mechanised agriculture.

definition.text: Physical and biological things found in the oceans that are useful to people.

facts.text: They include marine biodiversity, ecosystem services from coasts and coral reefs, minerals from deep sea mining, and marine renewable energy.
The term was popularised by Sustainable Development Goal 14, which aims to conserve and sustainably use the oceans, seas and marine resources.
Sustainable fisheries contributed around 0.1% of global GDP per year.

definition.text: Systems for grading mineral deposits by how well they are known and whether they can be mined at a profit.

facts.text: A mineral resource is material in or on the Earth's crust with reasonable prospects for eventual economic extraction.
Resources are split, in increasing geological confidence, into inferred, indicated and measured.
A mineral reserve is the economically mineable part of a measured or indicated resource, divided into probable and, with highest confidence, proved reserves.
Most schemes follow the CRIRSCO International Reporting Template, such as Australia's JORC Code; the UN Framework Classification for Resources dates from 1997.
Ores are concentrated unevenly, so extraction eventually meets diminishing returns as it moves to less accessible sites and lower grades.

definition.text: The economic rent earned from using natural resources such as minerals, oil reserves, rivers, waterfalls, coastal space and wind.

facts.text: It is the surplus left after selling a resource's output and paying all extraction and production costs, including a normal return.
Differential (Ricardian) rent comes from better sites: a coal firm with $20/t costs earns more rent than one with $30/t costs at the same price.
Scarcity (Hotelling) rent arises because extracting a finite resource today leaves less for later; if oil's price rises from $50 to $70 while costs stay $30, rent per barrel rises from $20 to $40.
Entrepreneurial rent, or quasi-rent, comes from management skill or investment that cuts costs or raises price.
Resource rents have been called a 'natural dividend' that should belong to the people who own the resources.
In fisheries, maximum economic yield is the catch at which resource rent is greatest; catching more counts as economic overfishing.
